summary.summary: West Berkshire's draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 is dominated by financial sustainability, described as 'extremely difficult' and corroborated by a CIPFA Financial Resilience review, external auditor KPMG, and the s151 Officer's own section 25 statement. The provisional 2025/26 outturn was £192.9m net expenditure against a £183.4m net budget; the council has again secured Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), which it stresses is short-term, must be repaid with compound interest, and is not a sustainable solution. The EFS requirement for 2025/26 has been reduced from £20m to £17m as the Finance Improvement Plan starts to bite (outturn improved £3.2m between Q3 and Q4; the DSG high-needs deficit improved £4.8m against forecast). Most striking for a lender: the AGS explicitly names a section 114 scenario as the risk if the DSG statutory override (in place to 31 March 2028) ends before the High Needs Stability Grant write-off of roughly 90% of the deficit materialises.

signals.headline: Exceptional Financial Support secured again for a second year to protect the General Fund; the £17m EFS requirement for 2025/26 is reduced from an earlier £20m estimate, but EFS 'must be repaid with compound interest' and is explicitly not a sustainable long-term solution (page 3-4)
signals.why: Continuing reliance on repayable exceptional support, even at a reduced level, means the underlying structural income/expenditure gap has not yet closed.

signals.headline: AGS states directly that if the DSG statutory override (protecting the balance sheet until 31 March 2028) ends before the High Needs Stability Grant write-off of circa 90% of the deficit lands, the council is exposed to 'catastrophic balance-sheet failure, resulting in a s114 scenario' (page 6)
signals.why: This is the council naming its own route to insolvency notice in a formal governance document, not an external commentator's inference.

signals.headline: High Needs (DSG) block deficit improved £4.8m against forecast outturn in-year, but remains kept off the general fund only by the statutory override to 31 March 2028; securing High Needs Stability Grant funding to write off circa 90% of it is the top-listed governance action for 2026/27-Feb 2027 (pages 4-6)
signals.why: The deficit is shrinking but the balance-sheet protection is time-limited and the write-off is not yet secured.

compliance.notes: Technically strong on the core prudential-indicator, liability-benchmark, MRP and affordability disclosures: full CFR reconciliation, liability benchmark charted over the full debt maturity profile and used as a live tool, detailed asset-life MRP policy, and a frank EFS-driven affordability/distress narrative (financing ratio breaching the 10% rule from 27/28). Weakest areas: no fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (RISK-02, core) despite repeatedly warning the Council is becoming 'fully exposed to interest rate risk'; commercial-investment proportionality asserted but not quantified (COM-03, core); and a cluster of absent items - no quantitative investment risk indicator (INV-06), no IMPs (COM-05), no guarantees/contingent-liability review (RISK-05), no derivatives policy (RISK-06), no ESG policy (ESG-01), no audit-qualification flag (RPT-05) and no third-party/pension monies attribution (GOV-07).

news_drafts.headline: West Berkshire schools funding forecast shows £13.55m deficit, £2.63m better than budgeted
news_drafts.lead:
West Berkshire Council's Schools Forum was told that the first-quarter forecast for the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools; a deficit is an overspend on it, usually on support for children with special needs) is a deficit of £13.55m. That is £2.63m better than the council budgeted for, according to the quarter-one monitoring report to the meeting on 12 October 2026.

The report describes the deficit as significant and underlying. It attributes the pressure to two areas: top-up funding for pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans, the legal documents setting out support for children with special educational needs, and the cost of places at Independent Non-Maintained Special Schools. The papers do not break the £2.63m improvement down further.

A separate briefing note covers a reconciliation the council carried out on how the grant's balances were reported. It compared figures across its Section 251 returns (the budget and spending statements councils send to the Department for Education), its statement of accounts (the formal annual accounts), its revenue outturn returns and its chief finance officer's assurance statements. The note says "DSG information reported in the Section 251 returns did not consistently align with other statutory returns and the Statement of accounts." The differences run from 2019/20 to 2024/25 and include mismatches between the closing balance for 2020/21 and the opening balance for 2021/22, and between opening and in-year balances in 2020/21. The council attributes them to errors in earlier reporting periods and states they are presentation and reporting consistency issues with no financial impact on the underlying grant position.

news_drafts.headline: West Berkshire forecasts £9.3m first-quarter overspend, £8.2m of it in children's social care
news_drafts.lead:
West Berkshire Council is £9.3m over budget after the first three months of 2026/27, according to the quarter-one financial report before its Executive on 24 September. Net spending stands at £220.2m against a budget of £210.9m, a variance of 4.4%. Children's social care accounts for £8.2m of it: £48.6m spent against a £40.5m budget, 20.2% over.

The report puts the pressure on residential care for children. The council budgeted for 24 annualised placements at £499,000 a year each; it now has 36, at £543,000. It forecasts a further five, costing about £3.0m. The report says the cost reflects the complexity of children's needs and "a national shortage of suitable residential placements for children with the most complex needs". Residential net cost has grown by 27% a year, compounded, over four years. The wider Children's Services directorate is £10.3m over, partly offset by £2.6m under on education funded by the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools).

One line has moved the other way. The budget assumed a £16.6m adjustment for the schools-grant deficit, but the quarter-one figure is £13.6m, £3.1m lower.

The overspend bears on the council's reserves, the money it has put aside. Its general reserve, a cushion for the unexpected, is just over £10m. The report says the quarter-one outturn would reduce it to about £1m, below the level the council's chief finance officer (the section 151 officer) recommends as sustainable. About £4.6m of reserves created through exceptional financial support, government permission to borrow to cover day-to-day spending, could lift it to about £5.6m. The council expects its total need for that support in 2026/27 to exceed the provisional £30m allocation, and any increase needs approval from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.

Borrowing is forecast to rise from £306.1m to £365.6m by March 2027 and £486m by March 2029. The annual minimum revenue provision, the amount set aside to pay off past borrowing, is forecast at £7.1m this year, up from £6.6m, and about £15.3m by 2032/33, of which £6.7m repays support-related borrowing.

Elsewhere, 24 affordable homes were completed in the quarter against a target of 37. The council expects more in the second and third quarters, towards 146 for the year.

news_drafts.headline: West Berkshire's first-quarter forecast puts its government-backed borrowing need at £40m against £30m agreed
news_drafts.lead:
West Berkshire Council's 2026/27 budget was approved with a £30m gap to be covered by exceptional financial support (EFS), which is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has provisionally agreed that sum. The first-quarter budget report to the Resources and Place Scrutiny Committee on 22 September forecasts the council ending the year £9.3m over budget. The paper says this "would effectively generate a £40m EFS gap".

The council applies for EFS each year in December and is notified in February. Any amount above the provisional £30m needs further approval from the ministry. The report says it would also mean higher capital financing costs in future years, meaning the cost of borrowing for long-lasting assets, unless these are covered from money the council has set aside.

The borrowing carries a repayment cost. Each year the council must set aside part of its budget to pay off past borrowing, much like a mortgage repayment, a charge known as minimum revenue provision. It is forecast at £7.1m for 2026/27, up from £6.6m in 2025/26. The paper projects it reaching about £15.3m by 2032/33, of which around £6.7m "relates to the repayment of borrowing associated with Exceptional Financial Support".

findings.headline: Education traded services income fell £0.2m as buy-back services ceased and school take-up declined
findings.detail: Traded services shows £0.2m adverse variance: £0.1m from cessation of Education Psychology and Emotional Health Academy buy-back services, and £0.1m from reduction in school Improvement buy-in.
findings.matters: Loss of traded services income signals either schools' budget constraints or loss of competitiveness; affects funding available for support services
findings.figures: £0.2m adverse variance (service cessation £0.1m, reduced school buy-in £0.1m)
findings.quote: Traded Services adverse variance +£0.2, +£0.1 due to the cessation of the Education Psychology buy back service and Emotional Health Academy buy back service.

findings.headline: Capital salary recharge reassessment reduced recharge income by £0.5m
findings.detail: Management and Strategy variance of £0.5m is driven by a capital salary recharge reduction following reassessment of allowable recharge levels. This suggests prior practice allowed higher recharge levels than now assessed as compliant.
findings.matters: A material reduction in inter-departmental recharges indicates prior budgets overstated cost recovery; the council now faces this as a permanent revenue cost correction
findings.quote: Management and Strategy adverse variance of +£0.5m, driven primarily by a capital salaries recharge reduction, based on a reassessment of allowable capital recharging in the team.

findings.headline: Special Education transport and services drove £1.1m of the £1.8m adverse variance
findings.detail: Home to School Transport overspend (£0.3m) is driven by increased Special Education transport costs. School Improvements and SEN Services overspend (£0.8m) comprises Special Needs Assessment Team agency costs (£0.1m), local outcomes framework investment (£0.4m), and Elective Home Education salary transfer (£0.1m).
findings.matters: SEN costs are a priority pressure for English councils; distinguishing between demand-driven overspend, strategic investment, and staffing pressure reveals budget sustainability
findings.figures: Home to School Transport +£0.3m, School Improvements and SEN Services +£0.8m (agency £0.1m, local outcomes framework £0.4m, Elective Home Education £0.1m)
findings.quote: Home to School Transport adverse variance of +£0.3m, primarily driven by an increase in Special Education Home to Schools transport costs.

findings.headline: Education service forecasts £1.8m adverse variance against budget in Q1
findings.detail: The Q1 Education forecast shows net expenditure of £11.27m with an adverse variance of £1.8m against budget. The variance is split across four service areas: Home to School Transport (£0.3m), School Improvements and SEN Services (£0.8m), Management and Strategy (£0.5m), and Traded Services (£0.2m).
findings.matters: Early-quarter overspend reveals whether the education budget is aligned with delivery costs; material variance at this stage signals year-end risk and informs council-wide resource planning
findings.quote: The Q1 Education forecast shows net expenditure of £11.27m, resulting in an adverse variance of £1.8m against budget.

findings.paper_title: 10. Early Years In Year Budget Position 2026-27 - Final
findings.headline: Early Years Q1 surplus revised from £0.7m to £0.1m following DfE post-year income adjustment
findings.detail: At Q1, West Berkshire forecast a surplus of £0.7m on income of £33.5m. In July 2026, the DfE confirmed the prior year (2025/26) income adjustment was a reduction of £0.2m, not the increase of £0.4m the council had forecast. This £0.6m swing reduced the 2026/27 adjusted position to a surplus of £0.1m. The council will absorb this reduction rather than passing it to providers.
findings.matters: Finance directors must understand how post-year funding adjustments can materially and unexpectedly change in-year positions mid-year, sometimes reducing financial headroom on pass-through budgets where forecast accuracy is challenging.
findings.figures: Forecast income £33.5m, forecast surplus £0.7m, 25/26 DfE adjustment £0.2m reduction, adjusted 26/27 surplus £0.1m
findings.quote: In July 2026, after quarter one had closed the Department for Education confirmed the 25/26 income adjustment was a reduction of £0.2m. This has resulted in a £0.6m reduction to the 26/27 Early Years Block position.
